# Diagnosing Cold Idle Roughness on the 6G72 V6

A rough idle lasting exactly two or three seconds during cold starts, followed by immediate stabilization, is a classic symptom of an air-fuel mixture imbalance that resolves once the engine control unit (ECU) warms up its sensors. This specific behavior isolates the problem to components involved in initial start-up enrichment or early warm-up logic rather than a mechanical failure affecting running conditions. Given your history with the 2003 Mitsubishi Montero Sport 6G72, where you recently replaced spark plugs, wires, top end seals, and cleaned the intake and injectors, we can narrow the search significantly.

Since a tune-up was performed and the engine runs perfectly after stabilization, mechanical friction issues like worn piston rings or valve guides are unlikely culprits. The fact that the car drives perfectly implies the ignition system and fuel delivery under load are functioning correctly. The issue is strictly transient. On the 6G72 platform, the most probable cause lies within the coolant temperature sensor (ECT) circuit or the Idle Air Control (IAC) valve.

The ECT sensor provides critical data to the engine computer to determine how much fuel enrichment is needed and what base idle speed is required. If this sensor sends a signal indicating the engine is colder than it actually is, the ECU will continue injecting extra fuel even after the coolant has reached operating temperature. However, since your issue resolves quickly, it suggests the sensor might be providing erratic readings initially or that the IAC valve is struggling to bypass enough air during that first few seconds before the throttle body warms up slightly.

You should inspect the resistance of the ECT sensor immediately. A common failure mode on older Mitsubishi engines is a cracked solder joint inside the sensor housing caused by thermal expansion cycles. This results in intermittent voltage spikes that confuse the ECU at startup. If the sensor is functional, the Idle Air Control valve is the next logical suspect. The IAC valve regulates airflow when the throttle plate is closed. On cold starts, it needs to open wider than normal to compensate for dense air. If the valve is partially clogged with carbon buildup from previous driving cycles, or if the stepper motor inside is sticking, the engine will run rough until the ECU detects the deviation and manually adjusts the fuel map to compensate. This compensation often takes a few seconds to manifest, matching your reported 2-3 second window.

Another factor to consider is the Mass Air Flow (MAF) sensor. Even after cleaning, if the internal heating element or the signal wire has developed high resistance, it might send an incorrect airflow reading during the first intake pulses of the cold engine. The ECU trusts the MAF over the IAC for initial air quantity estimation. If the MAF signal is momentarily weak or noisy, the mixture will lean out, causing that roughness.

Before replacing expensive parts like the ECT sensor, perform a visual inspection of the throttle body. Remove the air intake duct and check for carbon deposits around the bore where the IAC valve is mounted. While you have cleaned the intake systems recently, heavy carbon on the IAC pintle can prevent it from seating fully in the closed position initially. A gentle cleaning with a throttle body cleaner specifically designed for the IAC port can often resolve this without replacing the unit.

If these steps do not yield results, consider scanning the vehicle with an OBD-II interface to read live data streams. Look at the Coolant Temperature PID immediately after starting the engine. Does the value jump erratically before settling? If the ECU is reporting a coolant temperature of 80Â°C when it is actually -5Â°C, you have a sensor failure confirmed. Addressing this specific electrical fault is far more effective than replacing mechanical components that appear to be in good order.
